report:
**Conclusion: yes.** Denosumab (Prolia) *does* reduce vertebral-fracture risk—most directly established in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis.

The pivotal randomized, placebo-controlled FREEDOM trial gave denosumab 60 mg subcutaneously every six months for 36 months. New radiographic vertebral fractures occurred in **2.3%** of denosumab-treated participants versus **7.2%** with placebo: an absolute reduction of **4.8 percentage points** and a **68% relative risk reduction** (relative risk 0.32; statistically significant). It also reduced hip and nonvertebral fractures. https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/nejmoa0809493

This is not merely an isolated conclusion: the FDA label states that, in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis, Prolia reduces vertebral, nonvertebral, and hip-fracture incidence. https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2011/125320s5s6lbl.pdf

Important qualifications:

* The strongest direct fracture-outcome evidence is for **postmenopausal osteoporosis**; do not assume the same magnitude applies to every osteoporosis population without considering the relevant indication and individual risks.
* Benefit depends on continued, on-schedule therapy. Stopping denosumab can lead to rapid bone loss and reported **multiple vertebral fractures**; a clinician should plan transition to another antiresorptive treatment rather than simply stopping it. https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=49e5afe9-a0c7-40c4-af9f-f287a80c5c88
* Treatment choice also depends on fracture risk, kidney function, calcium/vitamin-D status, adverse-effect risks, and alternatives. The Endocrine Society recommends reassessing risk after 5–10 years and continuing or switching therapy if risk remains high. https://www.endocrine.org/clinical-practice-guidelines/osteoporosis-in-postmenopausal-women
